summary: Ezekiel 24 (27 verses) continues the story of glory. Starting with 'Again, in the ninth year, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,', it moves through themes of glory, idolatry and calls readers toward new heart.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows glory lived out in chebar canal, babylon. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: Again, in the ninth year, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, Yahweh’s word came to me, saying,

“‘“I, Yahweh, have spoken it. It will happen, and I will do it. I won’t go back. I won’t spare. I won’t repent. According to your ways and according to your doings, they will judge you,” says the Lord
In that day your mouth will be opened to him who has escaped, and you will speak and be no more mute. So you will be a sign to them. Then they will know that I am Yahweh.”

questions.question: What is happening in Ezekiel 24?
questions.answer: In 27 verses, this chapter ezekiel 24 (27 verses) continues the story of glory. starting with 'again, in the ninth year, in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month, yahweh’s word came to me, saying,', it moves through themes of glory, idolatry and calls readers toward new heart. The setting is chebar canal, babylon, written to exiles in babylon. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Ezekiel and why 24 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally ezekiel, addressed to exiles in babylon around ~593-571 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as visions, oracles — its themes of glory, idolatry build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'glory' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Visible weight of God's presence and honor. In this chapter, it appears in context of glory. For a first-time reader: think of it as visible weight of god's presence and honor, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through glory and idolatry, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 21 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: '‘Speak to the house of Israel, “The Lord Yahweh says: ‘Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the pride of your power, the desire of your eyes, and that which your soul pities; and y...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about glory. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
